newsitem.title: CANADA: Curb video lottery terminals - Canada govt panel.
newsitem.headline: Curb video lottery terminals - Canada govt panel.

text.p: A Canadian government panel on Monday recommended sharp restrictions on video lottery terminals (VLTs), saying they are easy for compulsive gamblers to use and are addictive.

"A shocking number of people are addicted to gambling," said Lucie Blais, acting chairwoman of the National Council of Welfare. "The last thing these people need is to come face to face with a VLT every time they go out."

VLTs are a video version of the so-called one-armed-bandit slot machines, and eight of Canada's 10 provinces have them. The government of Ontario, Canada's largest, plans to flood the province with 20,000 VLTs.

"No skill or knowledge is required to play. A single 'hit' costs very little, but playing tends to be addictive," the council, a publicly-funded citizens' advisory group to the federal minister of human resources development, said in a report.
It recommended that VLTs be banned except in casinos, which are present in seven provinces.
"We believe they have no place in bingo halls or race tracks, and they certainly have no place in restaurants and bars or any place accessible to young people," it said.
The report said Canadian studies of gambling suggest that 1.2 million of the country's 30 million people may be problem or pathological gamblers.
The federal government has taken a low profile in dealing with gambling, usually deferring to the provinces, which increasingly rely on lotteries, VLTs and casinos to raise funds.

The report said those three sources provided the governments of the 10 provinces and two territories with $4.56 billion Canadian ($3.34 billion U.S.) in net revenue in 1995 -- C$154 (U.S.$113) on average from each adult and child.
It amounted to 2.7 percent of total provincial and territorial revenue.

Citing studies showing problem gambling among young people was much higher than among adults, the council recommended the provinces impose stiff penalties for lottery retailers who sell to minors and operators who admit minors to gambling premises intended for adults.
It also recommended that the governments spend 10 percent or more of their net gambling revenues on preventing and treating gambling problems.
